name: Changthang
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog cites only Zeisler 2011/2018 classification comments; no phonology/grammar of Changthang located online

new_statements.quote: The dialects of the Western section, including the two Jangthang dialects spoken in the state of Jammu Kashmir have a pitch tone system generally with a two-way contrast (high and low). This is a major distinction with the neighoring dialects of Ladakh (except the Jangthang dialects) and Zangskar. [p. 236:] In Ladakh, the only territory where tonal dialects are found is the Jangthang areas of Nyoma and Durbuk, and along the gorges or rong of the upper Indus. These Jangkat and Rongkat dialects are in contact with the non-tonal dialects of Central Ladakh.
new_statements.citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages: an introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan. Vol. 1, Part 2. Paris: LACITO Publications.
new_statements.locator: sec. 9.9.6 'Phonological characteristics of the W section', Suprasegmental features, p. 603 (txt lines 16940-16945); supporting sec. 7.3 p. 236 (lines 4164-4167) and p. 619 (lines 17482-17486)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (20508 lines). Both quoted sentences are present verbatim at the stated locators: lines 16939-16942 (sec. 9.9.6 'Suprasegmental features', page-header '604' follows at line 16955, so p. 603): 'The dialects of the Western section, including the two Jangthang dialects spoken in the state of Jammu Kashmir have a pitch tone system generally with a two-way contrast (high and low). This is a major distinction with the neighoring dialects of Ladakh (except the Jangthang dialects) and Zangskar.' (the typo 'neighoring' is in the source); lines 4164-4167 (after the '236' page marker at line 4151, so p. 236): 'In Ladakh, the only territory where tonal dialects are found is the Jangthang areas o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Ladakh Changthang (Jangthang: Nyoma and Durbuk blocks) and upper-Indus Rong dialects are pitch-tone dialects with a two-way high/low contrast, unlike the rest of Ladakh; the source says nothing about word-stress placement in them. (Francke 1904 p. 364 independently reports that Rubshu 'exhibits the Tibetan tone system in its full development'.)
new_statements.exceptions: None for these dialects; the same book says (sec. 9.10.6 p. 626) that NW-section (Ladakh/Balti) languages lack distinctive suprasegmentals, but explicitly excludes the Jangthang dialects from that section (fn. 19 p. 235).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is at the level of dialect classification (word-level pitch tone), not a description of stress; no citation forms or minimal pairs are given for Changthang. Tournadre has an unpublished Nyoma corpus (2018, p. 609 line 11612) so the claim is partly first-hand, but the primary description of Kenhat phonology (Zeisler 2011) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog chan1309 = Changthang [cna], alt. names Byangskat, Rong, Rupshu, Stotpa, Upper Ladakhi; it covers the Ladakh Jangthang nomad dialects (Nyoma block: Chumathang, Nyoma, Hanle, Rupshu/Korzok; Durbuk block/Lalok: Trangtse, Shachukul, Chushul) and the upper-Indus 'Rong'/Kharu dialects (Gya-Miru, Gya-Sasoma) that hh.bib maps to cna. The quoted statement is Tournadre & Suzuki's 'Durbuk Jangpa' and 'Nyoma Jangpa' dialects (which they classify in their Western section, with Spiti) plus the 'Rongkat' upper-Indus gorge dialects; Leh Ladakhi (lada1244) and Zangskari (zang1248) are excluded and are non-tonal per the same source. Francke 1904's 'Rubshu' = Rupshu (Nyoma block).

sources.quote: The dialects of the Western section, including the two Jangthang dialects spoken in the state of Jammu Kashmir have a pitch tone system generally with a two-way contrast (high and low). This is a major distinction with the neighoring dialects of Ladakh (except the Jangthang dialects) and Zangskar. sources.locator: sec. 9.9.6 'Phonological characteristics of the W section', Suprasegmental features, p. 603 (txt lines 16940-16945); supporting sec. 7.3 p. 236 (lines 4164-4167) and p. 619 (lines 17482-17486)
sources.note: Sec. 9.9.6 p. 603: the two Ladakh Jangthang dialects (Durbuk Jangpa, Nyoma Jangpa) have a pitch-tone system with a two-way H/L contrast; sec. 7.3 p. 236: the Jangkat and Rongkat (upper-Indus gorge) dialects are the only tonal dialects in Ladakh; p. 619: 'They have developed tones and have not preserved initial consonantic clusters'. No statement on word stress for these dialects (sec. 7.3.3 'Stress', pp. 241-242, discusses Balti, Lhasa, Zhongu, mBalhag only).

sources.citation: Francke, A. H. 1901. Sketch of Ladakhi Grammar. Calcutta (JASB 70 Part I Extra No. 2).
sources.note: 'The Accentuation' pp. 6-7 (stem/first syllable stressed; a few disyllables stressed on the second) is stated for the Leh dialect (per LSI p. 53); the Rongpa dialect (upper-most Indus valley) is mentioned only for the rule 'r or s and p = f'. Not a Changthang statement.

sources.citation: Zeisler, Bettina. 2025. A little-known past tense marker of the northern Changthang dialects of Ladakh. Himalayan Linguistics 24(1): 37-57. doi:10.5070/H9.45388.
sources.note: Morphosyntactic paper on the Lalokpa (Durbuk block, Trangtse, Pangong) and Nyoma-block dialects; transcriptions mark low tone with an underline diacritic (e.g. /-ʧu̱ŋ/, Tra̱ngtse) but the paper contains no statement on tone or stress placement (only 'non-accentuated'/'deaccentuated' said of a grammaticalised auxiliary).

This variety shows a marked influence of Tibetan on its phonology'; no suprasegmental statement about it (the 1976 p. 14 'stress and tone... non-significant' remark is about Leh Ladakhi).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.) 1909. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. III Part 1 (Tibeto-Burman family: Tibetan dialects...). Calcutta. 'Ladakhi dialect' pp. 51-70.
sources.note: pp. 52-53: Francke's sub-dialects Sham, Leh, Rong; 'In Rubshu... a form of Central Tibetan is spoken'; Rong cluster reflexes and final -ng loss; p. 53 'Tones.—Like Balti and Purik, Ladakhi is generally speaking devoid of tones' but 'The dialect described... is that of Leh'; p. 55 'Changthang dialect' mentioned only for past-stem formation. No accent statement for Rong/Changthang.

sources.citation: Francke, A. H. 1904. A language map of West Tibet with notes. Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 73(1), No. 4: 362-367 + pl. vii.
sources.note: p. 362: Rong-dialect cluster reflexes (sg/rg > gh, sk/rk > h, sp/rp > f, etc.); p. 364: 'The dialect of Rubshu is of an entirely different character altogether; it is closely related to the Central Tibetan dialects and exhibits the Tibetan tone system in its full development... But the tone system has not yet become quite extinct in the Indus valley'. Nothing on stress placement.
